caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

attempts.label: CRCNS:bst-2
attempts.entry_title: A neural ensemble correlation code for sound category identification (Sadeghi et al. 2019)
attempts.summary: Most of the paper's main neural findings held up: inferior colliculus multiunit correlations identify sounds and categories in single trials well above chance, and scrambling channel order hurts the temporal classifier. With spectrum-equalized sounds the correlation classifiers stayed above chance and the spectrum classifier fell, though the values did not match. In the cochlear model the category correlation widths and diversity reproduced, but the stationarity values did not, the index's formula being lost from the text. The model classifiers reached similar maxima, their optimal resolutions held only in part, and the spectrum classifier tied the temporal one, on a component count the paper does not give. Two supplementary analyses could not be tested, lacking tone-pip and raw voltage recordings.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Sadeghi, Zhai, Stevenson and Escabi (2019) on CRCNS bst-2, which holds the analog multiunit activity of 35 inferior colliculus recordings in unanesthetized rabbits (13 sites listening to five natural sounds, 11 to their 1/f spectrum-equalized variants, 11 to six exemplars of three categories) and the 195 sounds of the paper's auditory model. It recomputes the stimulus-driven and noise correlations with a port of the paper's code, the single-trial correlation classifiers, and the model's correlation widths, stationarity and diversity, and the model's leave-one-sound-out category classifier.

notebooks.title: Auditory model classifier of the 195 model sounds (Figs 9 and 10)
Neural ensemble correlations and classifiers, paradigms 1 to 3
Auditory model correlations of the 195 model sounds

outcomes.statement: At the example paradigm 1 site, stimulus-driven temporal correlations are fast for crowd, water and fire (3.0, 3.0 and 3.9 ms wide at 50% of maximum; 5.9, 6.9 and 11.8 ms at 10%), the bird chorus has a sharp peak (5.9 ms half width) and a slow component (161.2 ms at 10%), and the snake has a 7.9 ms half width, 20.6 ms at 10%, and a periodic pattern of about 50 ms period at high-frequency sites.
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding neural ensemble correlation statistics to recognize sounds, paragraph 4; Figure 1K
outcomes.quote: The temporal correlations for the crowd, water, and fire sounds are relatively fast (3.0 ms, 3.0 ms, and 3.9 ms width at 50% of the maximum; 5.9 ms, 6.9 ms, and 11.8 ms width at 10% of the maximum). The bird chorus has a similar sharp temporal correlation (5.9 ms half width), but it also contains a broader and substantially slower component (161.2 ms, 10% width)
outcomes.notes: At P1_Site04, with the window of the paper's code (the first half of the raster, as NeuralExample.m computes Fig 1) and the channel-averaged stimulus-driven temporal correlation, all ten widths are within tolerance and crowd and water are narrower than fire at 50%. The snake's side peak is at 60.9 ms (channels 9 to 16), outside 50 +/- 5 ms, so 10 of 11 values match. Under the two windows the claims file names, the whole response and 1000 ms windows, 7 to 8 of 11 values match (partially reproduced by the criterion); the bird's 10% width is then 138.8 or 50.2 ms. With the median over channels, 8 of 11 match under every window. The notebook now prints the lines of NeuralExample.m that set this window (73 to 75, NS2 = floor(NS/2), sA = 1:NS2; 80, RASNMod = RASNA; 86 and 87, T0 at the centre and TwMod = floor((NSMod - 2 MaxLag - 2)/Fsd 1000)).
deviations: The window is taken from the paper's code, Code/Examples/NeuralExample.m, which computes Fig 1 from the first half of each raster (T0 at its centre, Tw = NS - 2 MaxLag - 2 samples), as the claims file's opening comment allows; the claims file's two readings are shown as variants.
The aMUA is at the files' 2034.5 Hz, so the lag step is 0.49 ms where the paper's 2 kHz gives 0.5 ms.

The channel order along the probe is not documented, so the high-frequency channels for the period are read as channels 9 to 16 and, as a variant, 1 to 8 (52 to 62 ms either way); reading (b), best frequency above 2 kHz, cannot be run without best frequencies.

outcomes.statement: Noise correlations are generally stronger than the stimulus-driven correlations, with spectral SNR from -26.0 to -0.9 dB (mean -11.0, SD 7.2) and temporal SNR from -26.1 to -4.1 dB (mean -6.0, SD 8.2).
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding neural ensemble correlation statistics to recognize sounds, paragraph 5
outcomes.quote: Noise correlations were also generally stronger than the corresponding signal correlations (spectral Signal-to-Noise Ratio [SNR]: range = −26.0 to −0.9 dB, −11.0 ± 7.2 mean ± SD; temporal SNR: range = −26.1 to −4.1 dB, −6.0 ± 8.2 mean ± SD)
outcomes.notes: Reading (a)(c)(e), whole window, 65 site and sound values, spectral SNR mean -11.8 dB (SD 8.0, range -34.0 to 1.0) and temporal mean -8.1 dB (SD 9.0, range -29.3 to 7.7); 97% and 88% of the values are below 0 dB. Both means are within tolerance under 15 of the 18 readings, but no reading puts more than two of the four range bounds within tolerance (per site averages, spectral -26.8 to -1.4 and temporal -26.6 to 1.2 dB in the whole window). At the example site alone the means are -4.3 and -1.9 dB.
deviations: The SNR formula is not in the text; the readings of the claims file (squared stimulus-driven over squared noise correlations, with and without the zero-lag diagonal, per site and sound or per site, all sites or the example) are all run, under three windows.

outcomes.statement: Stimulus-driven neural spectral correlations are partly predicted by the spectral correlations of a peripheral auditory model of the same sound (average r = 0.3 +/- 0.03), and significantly above the across-sound control (-0.04 +/- 0.02, one-tailed t test).
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding neural ensemble correlation statistics to recognize sounds, paragraph 4; S5 Fig, panels D and E
outcomes.quote: these neural correlations were stimulus-driven and frequency-dependent since they were partly predicted by the spectral correlations from a peripheral auditory model (see Materials and Methods ; average r = 0.3 ± 0.03, t test, p < 0.01

statistics.about: average same-sound Pearson r against zero

outcomes.notes: The test needs each recording channel's best frequency, from the tone-pip frequency response areas (Fig 1A, S5 Fig legend). The data set holds only the aMUA rasters to the natural sounds; its file list (data.tar.gz members) and description have no tone-pip recordings or best frequencies, and the channel order along the probe is not documented, so the model channels cannot be matched to recording channels.

outcomes.statement: Across the 13 paradigm 1 sites, noise correlations are more restricted in frequency and time and more consistent across sounds than stimulus-driven correlations, which are broader and stimulus dependent (a slow component for the bird chorus and a 20 Hz periodic component for the snake).
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding neural ensemble correlation statistics to recognize sounds, paragraph 6; Figure 2
outcomes.quote: The spectral noise correlations (collapsed along the diagonal) are consistent across sounds and more restricted in frequency ( Fig 2B ) than the corresponding stimulus-driven spectral correlations ( Fig 2A )
outcomes.notes: Over the 13 paradigm 1 sites, with widths at 50% of the maximum (reading (a)), the noise correlations are narrower than the stimulus-driven ones for 5 of 5 sounds in both domains under every window (whole window, spectral 1.8 to 2.0 against 6.6 to 9.1 channels, temporal 1.2 against 4.8 to 7.5 ms), and their SD across sounds is smaller in both domains (spectral 0.33 against 0.68, temporal 3.63 against 48.67). Under reading (b), the mean beyond 2 channels or 10 ms, noise is lower for 5 of 5 sounds spectrally but for 2 of 5 temporally, as the stimulus-driven temporal correlations of fire, water and snake fall below zero beyond 10 ms. The bird chorus keeps a stimulus-driven correlation of 0.22 at 50 ms (noise 0.05) and the snake a side peak at 55 ms.
deviations: Each site's collapsed curves are normalised by their value at offset 0 or lag 0 before averaging (the claims file's open step).

outcomes.statement: At the example site, randomizing the channel order of the temporal classifier lowers its single-trial accuracy at 1 s from 72% to 35%.
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding neural ensemble correlation statistics to recognize sounds, paragraph 8; Figure 3A
outcomes.quote: Doing so substantially reduces the temporal classifier performance from 72% to 35% for the longest sound duration measured (1 s; Fig 3A )
outcomes.notes: At P1_Site04, at 1 s, randomising the validation channel order lowers the temporal classifier by 20 to 40 points under every reading ((1a)(2a) 78.4 to 45.1%, (1a)(2b) 64.4 to 31.3%, (1b)(2a) 80 to 60%, (1b)(2b) 70 to 30%). The value with tonotopy is within tolerance under two readings, the value without it under none. Chance is 20%.
deviations: The decision rule (reading 1) and the choice of PCs (reading 2) are not settled by the paper; all four combinations are run. Reading (4) concerns the spectrum classifier only.

outcomes.statement: At the example site, the spectro-temporal classifier performs best, followed by the spectral and temporal classifiers; the noiseless classifier exceeds the single-trial one for the spectral and spectro-temporal classifiers, while for the temporal classifier the two are similar.
outcomes.source: Figure 3A legend; Results, Decoding neural ensemble correlation statistics to recognize sounds, paragraph 7
outcomes.quote: The combined spectro-temporal classifier has the highest performance, followed by the spectral and temporal classifiers
outcomes.notes: The single-trial order spectro-temporal >= spectral >= temporal holds under 4 of 8 reading combinations (for example (1a)(2b), a on the model data, 86.4, 77.7 and 64.4%). The noiseless rule holds under none; the noiseless spectral classifier is 12 to 21 points above the single-trial one under the (1a) readings, but the noiseless temporal classifier is 13 to 30 points below the single-trial one, not similar, and the noiseless spectro-temporal classifier is not always 5 points higher (60 to 100% depending on how a is chosen).
deviations: The noiseless classifier is run at the example site at 1 s only (500 ms shuffled model windows, 1000 ms shuffled validation windows, 100 each), which is what the criterion compares.

outcomes.statement: Across the 13 paradigm 1 sites, all four single-trial classifiers (spectro-temporal, spectral, temporal, temporal without tonotopy) perform above chance at 1 s, improve with sound duration, and the temporal classifier is degraded substantially when tonotopy is removed.
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding neural ensemble correlation statistics to recognize sounds, paragraph 9; Figure 3B
outcomes.quote: Across all sounds and classifiers, the average performance is above chance (red curves in Fig 3B ; t test, p < 0.01, tested at 1 s duration) and improves with increasing sound duration
outcomes.notes: Under every reading, across the 13 sites, the four single-trial classifiers exceed 20% at 1 s ((1a)(2a) spectro-temporal 77.8%, spectral 76.9%, temporal 68.7%, without tonotopy 43.1%; largest two-sided p 7.8e-07), each is higher at 1 s than at 62.5 ms, and removing tonotopy lowers the temporal classifier by 25.6 points (paired t = 7.87, p = 4.4e-06; 25.4 to 31.5 points under the other readings). The 4 sites of one animal and the 9 of the other show the same pattern.

outcomes.statement: Single-trial accuracy at 1 s exceeds chance for every sound and classifier except the snake sound with the temporal classifiers (p = 0.15 with tonotopy, 0.92 without).
outcomes.source: S6 Fig legend
outcomes.quote: The classification accuracy of the single-trial classifier at 1 s duration exceeded chance ( p < 0.05, t test) for all conditions except for the snake sound

statistics.about: all other sounds and classifiers against chance

outcomes.notes: Under reading (1a) with PCs chosen on validation, all 18 non-snake-temporal conditions exceed 20% at p < 0.05 across the 13 sites and the two snake temporal conditions do not (16 of 18 with the inner split). Under the (1b) readings, 16 to 18 of 18 exceed chance but a snake temporal condition does too, so the claim holds under the (1a) readings only. Under (1a)(2a) the snake temporal classifier without tonotopy is significantly below chance (12%, p = 0.012), where the paper gives p = 0.92; the criterion asks only that it is not above chance, so the outcome stands, and the notebook flags the difference.
deviations: The decision rule is not settled by the paper (reading 1); the outcome holds under (1a) and not under (1b), and the criterion takes any reading.

outcomes.statement: The optimal spectro-temporal classifier weights spectral and temporal cues about equally, with a median mixing coefficient of 0.6 (quartiles 0.5 and 0.7) for paradigms 1 and 2 and 0.5 (25th percentile 0.4) for paradigm 3.
outcomes.source: S9 Fig legend; Discussion, Contribution of spectral and temporal correlations, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: For paradigms 1 (original) and 2 (spectrum-equalized), the median value of alpha is 0.6 (25th and 75th percentiles are 0.5 and 0.7), and for paradigm 3 (categorization), the median value of alpha is 0.5 (25th percentile is 0.4)
outcomes.notes: Three of the 32 reading combinations put both medians within tolerance, all with a chosen on the validation data and paradigm 3 whole responses (a). With paradigm 2 from the half split (3a), (1b)(2a) gives the 24 paradigm 1 and 2 sites pooled median 0.70 (quartiles 0.40 and 0.90) and paradigm 3 median 0.50 (25th percentile 0.25). With paradigm 2 from whole responses (3b), (1a)(2a) gives pooled 0.70 and paradigm 3 0.40, which also meets the per-paradigm rule (paradigm 1 0.70, paradigm 2 0.70), and (1b)(2a) gives pooled 0.65 and paradigm 3 0.50. Pooled 0.70 and paradigm 3 0.40 are at the edge of the tolerance, pooled 0.65 and paradigm 3 0.50 are not. The result depends strongly on how a is chosen; with a fitted on the model data the paradigm 1 medians are 0.50 to 0.60, the paradigm 2 medians 0.20 to 0.50 and the pooled medians 0.40 to 0.60, but the paradigm 3 medians are 0.80 to 0.90; with a fitted on the validation data and the (1a) readings the paradigm 3 medians are 0.00 to 0.40. The per-site values spread from 0.0 to 1.0 (printed).
deviations: The paper says only that a maximises the log-likelihood; a is chosen on the summed log-posterior of the true sound, on the model data or on the validation data, over a grid of 0 to 1 in steps of 0.1, and both are shown. Paradigm 2 uses its half split classifier (reading 3a).

outcomes.statement: Correlations from thresholded MUA resemble those from aMUA (median r 0.81 spectral, 0.35 temporal) but are weaker and noisier; split-half reliability is higher for aMUA (0.98 and 0.83) than for tMUA (0.77 and 0.27).
outcomes.source: S10 Fig legend; Materials and methods, Electrophysiology, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: aMUA and tMUA spectral correlations are quite similar, as indicated by the relatively high Pearson correlation coefficient (tMUA versus aMUA, median = 0.81). For temporal correlations, the Pearson correlation between tMUA and aMUA was lower (median = 0.35)
outcomes.notes: Thresholded MUA needs the raw voltage traces (events 2 SDs above the noise floor). The data set holds only the aMUA envelopes downsampled to 2034.5 Hz; the notebook lists every member of the tar (281 files, code, documents, sounds and the 35 neural files) and every field of the neural files (Data.Param with AnimalNo, BlockNo and RecordDate, and Data.Sound), and none holds voltage traces or spike times, so four of the six values cannot be computed. The two aMUA split-half values can and match. With the time halves of NeuralExample.m (first and second 1.5 s) the median r between halves of the stimulus-driven correlations is 0.980 spectral and 0.830 temporal over the 65 paradigm 1 rasters (reading a; 0.980 and 0.842 over all 373 rasters, reading b), against 0.98 and 0.83; with odd and even trials as halves they are 0.996 and 0.986.

outcomes.statement: At the example paradigm 2 site, neural correlations for the original and 1/f spectrum-equalized sounds are very similar (Pearson r = 0.92 +/- 0.01 spectral, 0.72 +/- 0.07 temporal, over five sounds).
outcomes.source: Results, Differences in correlations statistics are not due to sound spectrum alone, paragraph 3; Figure 4A to 4D
outcomes.quote: Fig 4 shows that the neural correlations for both the original sounds and spectrum-equalized conditions of a single recording location are remarkably similar (Pearson correlation coefficient, r = 0.92 ± 0.01 for spectral, r = 0.72 ± 0.07 for temporal; mean ± SE)
outcomes.notes: At P2_Site11, over the five sounds, original against 1/f stimulus-driven correlations give spectral r = 0.930 +/- 0.019 (within 0.92 +/- 0.01) and temporal r = 0.898 +/- 0.022, higher than the reported 0.72 +/- 0.07 and outside 10% of it under every reading (0.875 to 0.900). The correlations are as similar as the statement says, or more, but the temporal value differs from the reported one. Lag 0 does not drive the high temporal r; without lag 0 it is 0.888, without lags within 5 ms 0.693 +/- 0.110 (inside 0.72 +/- 0.07) and without lags within 20 ms 0.661; per channel the median r is 0.952. Only the first of these is the claims file's measure.

outcomes.statement: Across the 11 paradigm 2 sites, neural correlations for original and 1/f sounds correlate at r = 0.95 +/- 0.02 (spectral) and 0.80 +/- 0.02 (temporal) for the same sound, and less across different sounds (0.85 +/- 0.02 and 0.57 +/- 0.01).
outcomes.source: Results, Differences in correlations statistics are not due to sound spectrum alone, paragraph 3; Figure 4E
outcomes.quote: Across recording locations, the neural correlations for the original and equalized sounds have an average Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.95 ± 0.02 for spectral and 0.80 ± 0.02 for temporal (mean ± SE)
outcomes.notes: Across the 11 sites (whole window, per-site means), same sound 0.879 +/- 0.033 spectral and 0.917 +/- 0.007 temporal, across sounds 0.818 +/- 0.035 and 0.639 +/- 0.011. Same-sound exceeds across-sound in both domains under every reading, but no value is within its stated SE and at most 3 of 4 are within 10% (first-half window), so neither rule of the criterion is met. The spectral values are lower and the temporal ones higher than reported.

outcomes.statement: At the example paradigm 2 site, classifiers trained on the original sounds and tested on the 1/f sounds keep high accuracy (63% spectral, 63% temporal, 71% spectro-temporal, above chance), while the spectrum (rate) classifier falls from about 94% on the original sounds to chance.
outcomes.source: Results, Differences in correlations statistics are not due to sound spectrum alone, paragraph 4; Figure 4F
outcomes.quote: the maximum performance exceeds chance ( p < 0.05, t test) and remains high (63% for spectral, 63% for temporal, 71% for spectro-temporal). Furthermore, although the spectrum (rate) classifier achieves very high accuracy approaching 94% for the original sound, accuracy drops to chance level when the spectrum is equalized
outcomes.notes: At P2_Site11, with the half split (3a) and reading (1a)(2a), the classifiers trained on the original sounds give 58% spectral, 65% temporal and 79% (a on model data) or 65% (a on validation data) spectro-temporal on the 1/f sounds, and the spectrum classifier gives 90% on the original sounds; with a on the validation data all four values are within tolerance, but the spectrum classifier on the 1/f sounds is 31%, not below 30%. With (1a)(2b) it is 29% and three of four values are within tolerance. The pattern (correlation classifiers above 40%, spectrum below 30% on 1/f) holds under (1a)(2b) with the half split and under (1a) with whole responses (3b). The within-site t tests over the five sounds give p 0.016 to 0.033 for spectral and temporal under (1a)(2a).

outcomes.statement: Across 11 paradigm 2 sites, the correlation classifiers stay above chance on the 1/f sounds at 1 s (spectral 48%, temporal 49%, spectro-temporal 58%), while the spectrum classifier exceeds all three correlation classifiers on the original sounds (90.0 +/- 2.0%) but falls to 27.0 +/- 1.0% on the 1/f sounds and does not substantially improve with duration.
outcomes.source: Results, Differences in correlations statistics are not due to sound spectrum alone, paragraph 5; Figure 4G and 4H
outcomes.quote: All three classifiers perform above chance for 1 s duration when the spectrum is equalized ( Fig 4H ; spectral = 48%, temporal = 49%, spectro-temporal = 58%; p < 0.01, t test)
outcomes.notes: Across the 11 sites the three correlation classifiers exceed 20% on the 1/f sounds at 1 s under every reading (two-sided p < 0.003), and the spectrum classifier falls from 90.0 +/- 2.2% on the original sounds to 30.0 +/- 1.3% on the 1/f sounds ((1a)(2a), half split), below every correlation classifier. At most 3 of the 5 values are within tolerance; temporal 54.0% is just outside 49 +/- 4.9% and the spectrum classifier on 1/f sounds is outside 27 +/- 1% under most readings (24.5 to 38.2%). The spectrum classifier rises from 24.7% at 62.5 ms to 30.0% at 1 s. With whole responses (3b) the temporal classifier reaches 76 to 84% on the 1/f sounds.

outcomes.statement: At the example paradigm 3 site, the first two principal components explain 95.6% of the variance of the spectral and 85.9% of the temporal neural correlations, and the three categories form distinct clusters.
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding neural correlation statistics in a three-category identification task, paragraph 3; Figure 8B and 8D
outcomes.quote: With two principal components, most of the response variance is explained (95.6% for spectral and 85.9% for temporal), and the three categories are highly clustered
outcomes.notes: At P3_Site04, with 1000 ms windows of single-trial correlations (reading b), two PCs explain 96.3% of the spectral and 85.3% of the temporal variance of the six-exemplar training set (96.3 and 85.5% over the five-exemplar folds), and a nearest-centroid rule in two PCs classifies 88.6% and 85.6% of held-out exemplar windows (chance 33.3%). With 1000 ms shuffled windows the values are 98.3 and 88.3%; with 500 ms shuffled windows (reading a) the temporal value is 77.0%, just outside the tolerance, and the spectral nearest-centroid accuracy 76.1%.

outcomes.statement: At the example paradigm 3 site, all correlation classifiers approach 100% correct categorization at 1 s, and the spectrum (rate) classifier reaches 94%.
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding neural correlation statistics in a three-category identification task, paragraph 4; Figure 8E
outcomes.quote: all classifiers (spectro-temporal, spectral, and temporal) show increasing performance with sound duration, and the categorization accuracy approached 100% when the sound is 1 s. The spectrum (rate code) classifier also achieves high accuracy in this categorization task (94% for 1 s duration)
outcomes.notes: At P3_Site04, under every reading, the three correlation classifiers reach 93 to 100% at 1 s and are higher than at 62.5 ms (50 to 83%); the spectrum classifier gives 91 to 94%. Under reading (a), (1a)(2a), spectro-temporal 95, spectral 93, temporal 98 and spectrum 94%.

outcomes.statement: Across 11 paradigm 3 sites, at 1 s the spectro-temporal classifier categorizes 96% of trials correctly, the temporal 95%, the spectral 91% and the spectrum (rate) classifier 91%, all above chance, and performance improves with duration.
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding neural correlation statistics in a three-category identification task, paragraph 4; Figure 8F
outcomes.quote: For 1 s sound duration, the spectro-temporal classifier is above chance and achieves on average a 96% maximum accuracy ( t test, p < 0.01), followed by the temporal classifier (95%, t test, p < 0.01) and spectral (91%, t test, p < 0.01)

statistics.test: t test against chance, each classifier

outcomes.notes: Across the 11 sites, under every reading, the four classifiers are within tolerance at 1 s and above 33.3% (reading (a), (1a)(2a), spectro-temporal 94.8, temporal 94.8, spectral 92.2, spectrum 93.3%; two-sided p < 1e-10), and each is higher at 1 s than at 62.5 ms. The 3 and 8 sites of the two animals give the same values.

outcomes.statement: In the cochlear model, the example speech sound has broad spectral correlations and a slow temporal correlation (64 ms half width), while the example water sound has diagonal spectral correlations and a fast temporal correlation (4 ms half width).
outcomes.source: Results, Average correlation statistics and diversity, paragraph 1; Figure 5
outcomes.quote: The temporal correlation structure in speech exhibits a relatively slow temporal structure (64 ms half width) ... By comparison, the water sound has a relatively fast temporal correlation structure (4 ms half width)
outcomes.notes: With the time average of the short-term autocorrelations at tau_W = 566 ms (reading ii a) and the channel-averaged curve, Human_Speech Sound_1 has a 64.5 ms and Flowing_Water Sound_1 a 4.0 ms half width (median over channels 70.0 and 4.1 ms). With the long-term correlation of the whole envelopes speech is 81.1 ms, outside the tolerance. The speech example's mean off-diagonal zero-lag correlation is 0.464 against 0.259 for water. Across the 15 speech sounds the widths are 57.3 to 86.3 ms, across water 3.5 to 7.3 ms.
deviations: Bandwidths follow the Methods' formula, 25 + 75(1 + 1.4 f^2)^0.69, where the paper's example code uses criticalbandwidth.m (94 + 71 f^1.5); envelopes are resampled to 1 kHz as the Methods say, where the example code keeps 3675 Hz.
The short-term correlation is sampled every tau_W / 4, a standard choice for a time average.

outcomes.statement: Water and wind sounds have fast temporal correlations (half widths 3.9 and 3.6 ms) and diagonal spectral correlations, while vocalizations have slow ones (speech 64.9 ms, dogs 76.3 ms, cats 117.3 ms) and more extensive spectral correlations.
outcomes.source: Results, Average correlation statistics and diversity, paragraph 2; Figure 6A and 6B
outcomes.quote: relatively fast temporal correlation structure (impulsive; correlation half width ... water = 3.9 ms; wind = 3.6 ms)
outcomes.notes: With the 566 ms short-term reading and the channel-averaged category mean curve, four of five half widths are within tolerance (flowing water 3.9, wind 3.9, speech 67.9, dogs 82.4 ms); cats are 160.9 ms against 117.3 +/- 11.7. Every vocalization is wider than water and wind under all four readings. The statement's spectral part is mixed; dogs, speech and cats have high mean off-diagonal correlations (0.484, 0.429, 0.388) and flowing water the lowest (0.265), but single bird songs are low (0.273), below wind (0.315).
deviations: As in fig5-speech-water-widths.

outcomes.statement: White noise has the lowest category diversity index; among natural sounds speech is lowest (CDI 0.12), crowd noise 0.15, wind 0.18, dogs 0.21, bird songs 0.29 and fire highest (0.39), with no clear trend between classes.
outcomes.source: Results, Average correlation statistics and diversity, paragraph 3; Figure 6C
outcomes.quote: Of all sounds in our database, white noise has the smallest diversity, which is expected given that white noise is wide-sense stationary. Of the natural sounds, speech has the lowest diversity (CDI = 0.12)
outcomes.notes: With norms not squared (reading c on a), five of six CDIs are within tolerance (single bird songs 0.373 against 0.29 +/- 0.029), speech is the lowest of the 13 categories, white noise is lower still (0.042), and the six keep the paper's rank order. With squared norms (readings a and b) the values are 2.4 (fire, single bird songs) to 7.7 (speech) times smaller (speech 0.016, fire 0.162) and none is within tolerance, though the rank order is the same.
deviations: White noise is generated (15 Gaussian noises of 10 s, fixed seed), as the data set does not hold it.
The CDI equation is lost from the text; the claims file's readings are all run, and only the one with norms not squared matches the reported values.

outcomes.statement: Environmental sounds other than fire (running water, waves, thunder, wind) are the most stationary natural sounds (SI = 0.49 +/- 0.04), vocalizations less so (0.28 +/- 0.04), speech is the least stationary category and white noise the most.
outcomes.source: Results, Short-term correlation statistics and stationarity, paragraph 3; Figure 7I
outcomes.quote: except for fire sounds, environmental sounds (including running water, waves, thunder and wind) tend to have the highest average SI (SI = 0.49 ± 0.04; mean ± SE)
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a), with environmental sounds flowing water, waves, thunder and rain, and wind, mean SI 0.719 +/- 0.048 against 0.49 +/- 0.04 reported, vocalizations 0.358 +/- 0.089 against 0.28 +/- 0.04; reading (b) gives 0.792 and 0.621, and adding bird chorus and speech babble gives 0.654 under (a). Speech has the lowest category mean and white noise the highest under both readings, and environmental sounds are more stationary than vocalizations, but neither value is within tolerance under any reading. With the bandwidths of the code's criticalbandwidth.m (94 + 71 f^1.5, verifier point 8) the values hardly change (reading (a) 0.717 and 0.358, reading (b) 0.791 and 0.621; per-sound SI differences -0.011 to +0.007), so the bandwidth formula does not account for the gap.
deviations: As in fig5-speech-water-widths; the SI equation is lost from the text and the claims file's two readings are run.

outcomes.statement: In the 13-category model task, the spectral and temporal correlation classifiers perform best at a window resolution of 141 ms and the spectro-temporal classifier at 100 ms, and all perform above chance (7.69%) at every resolution.
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding sound-correlation statistics to categorize sounds, paragraph 2; Figure 9A
outcomes.quote: The optimal window resolution for both the temporal and spectral classifiers is 141 ms, while the optimal resolution for the joint spectro-temporal classifier is slightly faster (100 ms). Classification performance is above chance for all temporal resolutions tested ( Fig 9A ; chance performance = 7.69%; p < 0.01, t test, Bonferroni correction)
outcomes.notes: Changed from reproduced after verification round 3, which agreed with the change proposed after round 2. Under readings (6b) (windows spaced by the full Kaiser length) and (7b) (the reported PC and component counts), the spectral and temporal classifiers are best at 141 ms (82.1 and 80.5% at the full duration) and the spectro-temporal maximum (81.5%, 159 of 195 sounds) is tied. The tie changes from machine to machine. Of the five runs of the notebook in rounds 2 and 3, three (the last two among them) gave 81.0% at 100 ms and a tie at 141 and 283 ms, and two gave 81.5% at 100 ms as well, a three-way tie at 100, 141 and 283 ms in which ties going to the first grid point put both optima on the reported points; the runs differ by one sound at a few resolutions, a floating-point difference that moves marginal decisions. Either way the data do not single out 100 ms. In a bootstrap over sounds the spectro-temporal maximum falls at 283 ms in 27 to 29%, at 141 ms in 20 to 24% and at 100 ms in 15 to 19% of resamples, and the tie-breaks disagree (posterior of the true category 81.54% at 283 against 81.40% at 141 ms; mean accuracy at 1, 2, 4 and 8 s 71.2% at 283 against 77.1% at 141 ms, and 77.2% at 100 ms in the three-way tie). 141 ms is within one grid step of 100 ms, which meets the partial rule; 283 ms is not. Under (6a)(7b) the optima are 283, 141 and 141 ms, and under the (7a) readings the spectro-temporal optimum is 283 ms. Every correlation classifier is above 7.69% at every resolution under every reading (lowest 58.5%, temporal at 25 ms; largest Bonferroni p over the 195 per-sound outcomes 1.3e-31, over the 13 category means 7.9e-05). The accuracy curves over resolution are flat (spectral 72 to 82%).
deviations: The classifier is the Methods' pipeline, with choices the paper does not make, stated in model.py and the notebook; the spectro-temporal feature vector is the spectral and temporal features of a time point side by side; PCA is fitted once on all 195 sounds (refitted per fold for 26 folds as a variant, 80.8% against 76.9%); training observations are subsampled to 10000 per category, equally from each sound; the spectrum classifier, whose counts the paper does not give, uses the PCs for 90% and 8 components.

Reading (7a) uses the PCs explaining 90% at each resolution with the reported N_c; the cross-validated choice of N_c (over 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 and 20 components, a subset of the Methods' 1 to 20, for time) was run at each (6a)(7b) optimum only, giving 3 (reported 8) for spectral, 20 (reported 5) for temporal and 13 (reported 13) for spectro-temporal.

Where accuracies tie at the optimum the first resolution is taken (an assumption, as the paper reports one optimum); every tied resolution is listed, with two tie-breaks and a bootstrap, and the claims that use the spectro-temporal optimum are recomputed at each tied resolution.

outcomes.statement: At about 10 s the three correlation classifiers reach similar performance (spectro-temporal 84%, spectral 83%, temporal 81%), with no significant pairwise differences.
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding sound-correlation statistics to categorize sounds, paragraph 2; Figure 9B
outcomes.quote: all three classifiers achieve similar maximum performance at approximately 10 s (spectro-temporal = 84%, spectral = 83%, temporal = 81%; spectral versus temporal ... p = 0.60 ... spectral versus spectro-temporal ... p = 0.79 ... temporal versus spectro-temporal ... p = 0.42; two-sample t test)
outcomes.notes: Each classifier at its own optimum and the full duration, under (6b)(7b) the spectro-temporal classifier is 81.5%, spectral 82.1% and temporal 80.5%, all within tolerance, and no pair differs (two-sample t tests over the 195 per-sound outcomes, p 0.70, 0.90 and 0.80; over the 13 category accuracies p 0.84 to 0.95); the same at either tied spectro-temporal resolution. Under (6a)(7b) the values are 83.1, 82.1 and 80.0% (p 0.43 to 0.79). Under (6a)(7a) the spectro-temporal classifier reaches 87.7% and differs from the temporal one (p = 0.04 over sounds, 0.27 over categories), so the absence holds under the (7b) readings, the reported counts, and under (7a) with (6b) (p 0.18 to 0.70).
deviations: As in fig9a-optimal-resolution.

outcomes.statement: The spectral classifier reaches 90% of its maximum faster than the temporal one (1.7 against 3.0 s), and the spectro-temporal classifier fastest (1.2 s).
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding sound-correlation statistics to categorize sounds, paragraph 2; Figure 9B
outcomes.quote: the spectral classifier performance increases at a faster rate than the temporal classifier (reaching 90% of maximum in 1.7 versus 3.0 s; Fig 9B ) ... The joint spectro-temporal classifier improves at an even faster rate (reaching 90% of its maximum in 1.2 s)
outcomes.notes: No reading puts all three rise times within tolerance. The order spectro-temporal < spectral < temporal holds under the (7b) readings and (6a)(7a) for every way of measuring it; under (6a)(7b) every optimum is unique (spectral 283, temporal and spectro-temporal 141 ms), so it does not rest on a tie there. Under (6b)(7b), with the spectro-temporal classifier at 141 ms, linear interpolation gives spectral 1.92 s (1.7 +/- 0.17), temporal 2.67 s (3.0 +/- 0.3) and spectro-temporal 0.85 s (1.2 +/- 0.12); the first sampled duration 2.31, 3.08 and 1.16 s (two of three within tolerance); an exponential fit 1.45, 1.90 and 0.73 s. In the runs where 100 ms ties for the spectro-temporal optimum and is taken, its rise time is 1.23 s interpolated and 1.65 s first sampled (one of three within tolerance). With it at the tied 283 ms its rise time is 3.42 s and the order fails. Under (6a)(7b) the times are shorter (0.6 to 1.9 s). Under (6b)(7a) the spectro-temporal classifier (at 283 ms) is no faster than the spectral one.
deviations: As in fig9a-optimal-resolution.

outcomes.statement: Ignoring nonstationary structure by averaging the spectro-temporal statistics over time reduces category identification performance by about 25%.
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding sound-correlation statistics to categorize sounds, paragraph 2; Figure 9C
outcomes.quote: ignoring the nonstationary structure of the spectro-temporal correlation by averaging the statistics over time reduced the sound category identification performance by approximately 25%
outcomes.notes: At the spectro-temporal optimum and the full duration, reading (a) (time-averaged category models, one diagonal Gaussian per category) is 5.1 to 6.7 points below the short-term classifier under every reading ((6b)(7b) at 141 ms 74.9 against 81.5%; 6.0 to 8.2% relative), not 25. Reading (b) (the running average of the test sound scored under the short-term models) is 15.4 to 33.8 points lower ((6b)(7b) 51.8 against 81.5%, 29.7 points, 36.5% relative), and 36.9 points at 100 ms in the runs where 100 ms ties for the spectro-temporal optimum. No reading gives 25 +/- 2.5 at the optima used; the time-averaged classifier is at least 10 points lower under reading (b) only, which meets the partial rule. With the spectro-temporal classifier at the tied 283 ms under (6b)(7b), reading (b) is 25.6 points lower, within 25 +/- 2.5, and reading (a) 1.0 point, so the outcome also rests on the tie-break of fig9a-optimal-resolution. The outcome rests on reading (b), whose test feature differs from the training features of the models.
deviations: As in fig9a-optimal-resolution. Reading (a) uses N_c = 1, as a category has only 14 or 15 time-averaged vectors, and the vectors are the time averages of the short-term PC scores.

outcomes.statement: Some categories are identified much better by one feature set; waves by spectral correlations (100% against 33%) and wind by temporal ones (47% against 80%).
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding sound-correlation statistics to categorize sounds, paragraph 3; Figure 9D and 9E
outcomes.quote: Certain sounds such as waves perform substantially better for the spectral classifier (spectral = 100% versus temporal = 33%). Other sounds, such as wind, exhibit higher performance with the temporal classifier (spectral = 47% versus temporal = 80%)
outcomes.notes: Under (6a)(7b), waves are 100% with the spectral and 33.3% with the temporal classifier and wind 33.3% and 80.0%; three of four values are within tolerance (wind spectral 33.3 against 47 +/- 6.7). Under the (6b) readings waves temporal and wind spectral are both 40.0% (two of four). Under every reading waves are better identified by spectral and wind by temporal correlations by at least six sounds of 15, which meets the partial rule.
deviations: As in fig9a-optimal-resolution.

outcomes.statement: The spectrum-based classifier does not depend on temporal resolution and performs below all three correlation classifiers.
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding sound-correlation statistics to categorize sounds, paragraph 4; Figure 9A and 9B
outcomes.quote: Unlike the correlation-based classifiers, performance of the spectrum-based classifier does not depend on the temporal resolution of the analysis ( Fig 9A ) ... Furthermore, the overall performance of the spectrum classifier is lower than the either of the three correlation-based classifiers ( Fig 9B )
outcomes.notes: The spectrum classifier (windowed mean envelope of each channel, PCs for 90% and 8 components) varies by 9.7 to 10.3 points over the ten resolutions (70.3 to 80.5% at the full duration) and is best at the shortest windows, 25 or 50 ms, where it reaches 80.0 to 80.5%. At the full duration it ties the temporal classifier exactly under every reading (margin +0.0; (6a)(7b) 80.0% against temporal 80.0% and spectral 82.1%), so the partial rule fails by zero points, and it is above the temporal classifier at most durations (below at 2 to 4 of 10 to 12). Neither the full nor the partial rule is met. The outcome rests on the component count, which the paper does not give. With 13 components, the count the Methods' rule (cross-validated likelihood, which the Spectrum-based classifier section's "identical model generation" points to) picks at 25 ms, the result is the same (range 10.8 to 11.3 points, temporal margin -1.0 or +0.0). With 5 components it is below all three at the full duration under every reading (margins +1.5 to +9.2) and varies by 7.2 points, which would meet the partial rule.
deviations: As in fig9a-optimal-resolution. The spectrum classifier's PC and component counts are not given; the PCs for 90% (5 to 8) and 8 components are used, an assumption; 13 (the cross-validated choice) and 5 components are run as variants.

outcomes.statement: In a vocalization against background task, the spectro-temporal classifier approaches 90% for background and nearly 100% for vocalizations; vocalization accuracy improves with duration while background accuracy stays constant, and vocalizations are classified better with spectral than temporal correlations.
outcomes.source: Results, Decoding sound-correlation statistics to categorize sounds, paragraph 5; Figure 10
outcomes.quote: The model performance is consistently high, with accuracy rates for the spectro-temporal classifier approaching 90% for background sounds and nearly 100% for vocalizations ( Fig 10 )
outcomes.notes: Changed from reproduced after verification round 3, which agreed with the change proposed after round 2. Under (6b)(7b) and reading (a) (one GMM per class), with all three classifiers at 141 ms, the spectro-temporal classifier is 94.8% for background and 98.3% for vocalizations at the full duration, vocalization accuracy rises from 91.7%, background stays within 85.9 to 95.6%, and the temporal classifier is 23.2 points below the spectro-temporal one on vocalizations averaged over matched durations (reading d; 25.0 at the full duration, reading c), outside -20 +/- 2. In the runs where 100 ms ties for the spectro-temporal optimum (fig9a-optimal-resolution) and is taken as the first of the tie, the values are 93.3 and 96.7%, vocalizations rise from 81.7%, background stays within 87.4 to 94.1%, and the matched difference is -21.1 over 9 durations (-23.3 at the full duration), within the tolerance; that is the one reading that meets the full rule, and it does so only through the choice of 100 ms from the tie, which the data do not support and which three of five runs do not give. With the tied 283 ms the matched difference is -17.3. Spectral beats temporal on the vocalizations at every matched duration (90.0 against 73.3% at the full duration) but at Bonferroni-corrected p < 0.01 (paired t test over the 60 vocalizations) at 1 of 10 durations only (p = 9.1e-3). Under (6a)(7b) reading (a), where every optimum is unique (spectral 283 ms, the others 141 ms), the values are 94.8 and 98.3%, vocalizations rise from 91.7%, background stays within 85.2 to 94.8%, the difference is -25.0 (c) and -24.3 (d), and spectral beats temporal at p < 0.01 at 8 of 10 matched durations. Under reading (b) (13-category decisions mapped to the class) the temporal classifier reaches 96.7 to 98.3% on vocalizations and the difference is -1.7 to -11.8 points. The duration trends and the spectral advantage hold under every reading and the difference is out of tolerance except with the spectro-temporal classifier at 100 ms, which meets the partial rule.
deviations: As in fig9a-optimal-resolution. The class models use the 13-category classifier's PC and component counts. The curves of two classifiers are compared at matched durations (the temporal curve interpolated at the spectro-temporal durations for reading d; for the paired tests, the temporal outcome at the longest duration not exceeding each spectral one).

findings.statement: The aMUA rasters are sampled at 2034.5 Hz (12207.03 Hz divided by 6, the Fs field of every file), where the paper states 2 kHz; 6104 samples per trial make the stated 3 s only at the files' rate. The data description gives no rate.

The data set holds only the aMUA rasters to the natural sounds. The tone-pip recordings and best frequencies behind Fig 1A and S5 Fig, and the raw voltage traces behind the thresholded MUA of S10 Fig, are not deposited, so those analyses cannot be repeated.

The order of the 16 channels along the probe (which end is dorsal, low frequency) is not documented, so the channels cannot be assigned to frequencies, and the Param.RecordDate field holds values such as May2019 and May2019C2 without explanation.

P2_Site08 has 13 trials per sound, where the paper states one paradigm 2 site with 14 trials and all others with 20. The other trial and site counts match the paper (paradigm 1 18 to 39 trials, 13 sites, 4 and 9 per animal; paradigms 2 and 3 11 sites each, 3 and 8 per animal).

The data description says all sound files are double precision WAV; the 195 model sounds are 16 bit integer PCM and the paradigm sounds 32 bit float. The model sounds' SD is 0.0003 to 0.0022 of full scale, where the description says they are normalised to 0.001.

The whole data set is one 5.3 GB tar.gz file, which cannot be read at random; reading any neural file means decompressing the stream from the start (about 4 minutes for the whole file here). The white noise control of the model analyses is not included.

paper_notes.statement: The paper's model example code (ModelExample.m) builds the cochleogram with criticalbandwidth.m, b = 94 + 71 f^1.5 (f in kHz), where the Methods give b = 25 + 75(1 + 1.4 f^2)^0.69, and it keeps the envelopes at 3675 Hz (oversampling factor 4) where the Methods say 1 kHz. The Methods are followed here.

For the authors. The neural classifier's Methods leave open how the 100 random time samples enter a decision (each sample a decision, or log-likelihoods summed over the 100 samples for one decision), how the number of PCs that "maximize the classifier performance" is chosen (on the validation data or within the model data), and on which data the mixing coefficient a is fitted. The per-sound result of S6 Fig holds only when each sample is a decision, and the median a of S9 Fig changes from 0.0 to 0.9 with these choices. Which rules were used?

For the authors. The CDI of Fig 6C matches the reported values only when the norms are not squared (speech 0.123 against 0.12), while the Methods' prose (variance normalised by power) reads as squared norms, which give values 2.4 to 7.7 times smaller. The SI of Fig 7I under either squared reading gives higher values than reported (environmental 0.72 against 0.49). Which forms of the SI and CDI were used?

For the authors. The deposit holds no code for the model classifier of Figs 9 and 10, and the Methods leave open how the spectro-temporal feature vector is formed (taken here as the spectral and temporal features side by side), how the test windows are spaced (tau_W or the full Kaiser window), whether the PC and component counts were refitted at each resolution, and how the time-averaged classifier of Fig 9C was built, and the spectrum classifier's PC and component counts. The optimal resolutions and the Fig 9C reduction change with these choices (spectro-temporal optimum 100 to 283 ms; reduction 1 to 37 points), and the spectrum classifier is below all three correlation classifiers at 10 s with 5 components but not with 8 or 13. Which were used?

entries.name: sadeghi-2019
entries.title: A neural ensemble correlation code for sound category identification (Sadeghi et al. 2019)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Sadeghi, Zhai, Stevenson and Escabi (2019) on CRCNS bst-2, which holds the analog multiunit activity of 35 inferior colliculus recordings in unanesthetized rabbits (13 sites listening to five natural sounds, 11 to their 1/f spectrum-equalized variants, 11 to six exemplars of three categories) and the 195 sounds of the paper's auditory model. It recomputes the stimulus-driven and noise correlations with a port of the paper's code, the single-trial correlation classifiers, and the model's correlation widths, stationarity and diversity, and the model's leave-one-sound-out category classifier.
